explanation: Oral polio drops given in the field — by international 'STOP' teams working with local staff — are the classic instrument of global disease campaigns: cheap, easy to administer, and aimed at wiping out a preventable disease population-wide.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Oral polio drops are a vaccine, not an antibiotic; antibiotics treat bacterial infections and do nothing against viruses like polio.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The photo shows a mass immunization effort in the field — international health workers and local assistants vaccinating children against a preventable disease.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. This is a free, open-air, door-to-door style campaign, the opposite of an exclusive hospital treatment.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The workers are administering a modern vaccine, not traditional remedies.

options: (A) The use of antibiotics to cure viral infections, since penicillin and similar drugs are the standard medical treatment for polio and other viruses.
(B) Mass immunization campaigns, often organized with international support, targeting preventable diseases in developing countries.
(C) A hospital-based treatment available only to the wealthy.
(D) Traditional healers replacing modern medicine.
stem: The scene best illustrates which approach to disease in the global age?
stimulus: Photograph, India: a health worker gives oral polio vaccine drops to a young boy while an assistant steadies him; a vaccine carrier sits on the wooden table.

explanation: Before antibiotics, a simple bacterial infection could kill; after penicillin's mass production, pneumonia, wound infections, and childbed fever became routinely curable — a major reason death rates collapsed in the twentieth century.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Antibiotics kill bacteria, not viruses; polio and smallpox are viral and were conquered by vaccines, not penicillin.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Humans used herbal and other remedies for millennia; penicillin was the first modern antibiotic, not the first medicine.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Mass-produced penicillin made once-deadly bacterial infections treatable, driving a large share of the twentieth century's mortality decline.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Antibiotics treat infections; they do not prevent them the way vaccines do, so vaccination remained essential.

options: (A) provided a cure for viral diseases such as polio and smallpox, wiping out those epidemics decades before vaccines for them were ever developed.
(B) were the first medicines ever used by humans.
(C) made bacterial infections — once major killers — widely treatable, contributing to the twentieth century's plunge in death rates.
(D) eliminated the need for vaccines.
stem: Fleming's discovery, mass-produced during World War II, is most significant because antibiotics
stimulus: Color photograph, 1940s: Alexander Fleming, the discoverer of penicillin, at his laboratory bench holding a petri dish among culture plates and flasks.

explanation: The map's darkest reds (10–20%+) are confined to southern Africa while nearly the whole rest of the world is below 0.5%: HIV/AIDS became a disease of poverty and inequality, concentrated where health systems were weakest.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The map shows extreme concentration in southern Africa and near-zero rates elsewhere — the opposite of even distribution.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. North America and Europe are among the palest regions (below 0.2%); the highest rates are in poor southern African countries.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Tens of millions still live with HIV; the map documents its 2023 prevalence, not its eradication.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Despite medical advances, HIV remained brutally concentrated in southern Africa — a newer epidemic layered onto older patterns of global health inequality.

options: (A) HIV was distributed evenly around the world by 2023, with every region and continent showing roughly the same share of the population living with the virus.
(B) Wealthy countries had the highest HIV rates.
(C) HIV had been eradicated by 2023.
(D) Newer epidemics like HIV/AIDS remained brutally concentrated in poorer regions, especially southern Africa, even as other diseases were conquered.
stem: The map best supports which claim about disease in the global age?
stimulus: World map, 2023: share of the population aged 15–49 living with HIV. The darkest shades (10–20% or more) cover southern Africa — South Africa, Eswatini, Lesotho, Botswana, Zimbabwe; nearly everywhere else is below 0.5%.

explanation: Child death is now rare in wealthy countries (below 0.5%) but still reaches 10–20% in parts of West and Central Africa, with South Asia in between: the great health gains of the modern era were real but distributed by wealth.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The stark gradient — pale rich world, dark West and Central Africa — shows child survival still tracking poverty despite overall global progress.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Rates range from under 0.5% to 10–20%; the map's entire message is how unequal they are.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The palest (lowest-mortality) countries are North America, Europe, and Australia — the wealthy world, not the reverse.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Vaccines and other interventions drove the historic fall in child deaths; the map shows where that fall is incomplete, not that it never happened.

options: (A) Life-saving gains reached some regions far more than others, with child survival still closely tied to poverty.
(B) Child mortality is now the same everywhere in the world.
(C) Wealthy countries have the highest child mortality rates.
(D) Vaccines had no effect on child survival, since immunization programs never reached the developing world at any point in the twentieth century.
stem: The pattern shown best illustrates which limitation of twentieth-century health advances?
stimulus: World map, 2023: share of newborns dying before age five. The darkest shades (10–20%) cover West and Central Africa (Niger, Chad, Nigeria, CAR, Sierra Leone); South Asia is 2–5%; North America, Europe, and Australia are below 0.5%.

explanation: Every regional line climbs — most steeply after 1900 — and the lowest line gains the most, compressing the gap between regions: a story of global convergence in survival. The brief dip around 2020 (the COVID-19 pandemic) shows even long-run progress can be knocked back.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The lines climb steeply from 1900 onward, roughly tripling — the chart's entire story is dramatic change, not flatness.
option_explanations.B: Correct. All regions rise, the poorest most of all (narrowing gaps), and the small dip around 2020 marks the pandemic's interruption of the trend.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The lowest line — the poorest region — shows the largest gains; progress was fastest where life expectancy started lowest.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Birth rates do not change life expectancy at birth; the dip reflects excess deaths — the COVID-19 pandemic — not fewer births.

options: (A) Life expectancy has been flat for most of human history, including the entire twentieth century, with no region on earth gaining more than a year or two since 1900.
(B) Life expectancy rose worldwide in the modern era, with the poorest regions gaining the most — though the dip around 2020 shows progress can be interrupted.
(C) Only wealthy regions saw any gains in life expectancy after 1900.
(D) The dip around 2020 was caused by declining birth rates.
stem: Which conclusion is best supported by the chart?
stimulus: Line chart, 1770–2023: each colored line traces a world region's life expectancy at birth. All lines rise, especially after 1900; the lowest line climbs the most, narrowing the gap between regions; around 2020 several lines dip briefly.

explanation: The UN's medium-fertility projection shows India passing China around 2023 and peaking near 1.7 billion, China falling to about 600 million by 2100, and Nigeria surging to about 450 million: the demographic future belongs to South Asia and Africa, not East Asia.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. India's line stays above China's after about 2023 and keeps rising for decades; China does not retake the lead.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. China, Japan, and Brazil all decline in the projection; only India, Nigeria, and the US keep growing to 2100.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The chart's projections concentrate future growth in India and Nigeria (South Asia and Africa) while China's population shrinks steeply.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Nigeria reaches about 450 million by 2100 — large, but far below India's roughly 1.5 billion.

options: (A) China will remain the world's most populous country through 2100, staying well ahead of India and every other country in each decade shown in the projection.
(B) Every large country's population will keep growing through 2100.
(C) Future population growth will be concentrated in South Asia and Africa, while China's population is projected to shrink dramatically.
(D) Nigeria's population will surpass India's by 2050.
stem: The projections best support which claim about the future of population growth?
stimulus: Line chart, 1800–2100, of the most populous countries (UN medium-fertility projection). India overtakes China around 2023 and peaks near 1.7 billion around 2060; China declines steeply to about 600 million by 2100; Nigeria climbs to about 450 million; Japan, Brazil, and others level off or decline.

explanation: In 1975 about 84% of young men but only 69% of young women could read and write; by 2022 both were around 90% — schooling expanded for everyone, but girls' gains were larger, nearly erasing the gap.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Both lines climb steadily for nearly fifty years; attendance and literacy expanded, not declined.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. A roughly 3-point gap remains in 2022; the gap narrowed dramatically but was not eliminated by 1990 — or even by 2022.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Rising literacy means more reading and writing, not less; digital media did not reverse the trend.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The female line rises faster than the male line, closing a 15-point gap to about 3 points — the signature of mass schooling reaching girls.

options: (A) A decline in school attendance worldwide.
(B) The elimination of all gender differences in education by 1990, when girls' literacy caught up with boys' completely and the gap vanished forever.
(C) Literacy falling as digital media replaced reading.
(D) The massive expansion of schooling, especially for girls, narrowing the gender gap in basic education.
stem: The trend shown best reflects which social change of the late twentieth century?
stimulus: Line chart, 1975–2022: literacy rates of young men and women (ages 15–24) worldwide. Men's rate rises from about 84% to about 93%; women's from about 69% to about 90%, nearly closing a 15-point gap.

explanation: Nearly 380 million tonnes of new plastic in a single year — led by polypropylene and polyethylene — shows an economy built on cheap petrochemicals: the material base of disposable consumer culture, and a mounting waste crisis.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The sheer volume — hundreds of millions of tonnes of petroleum-derived polymers — documents how deeply mass consumption depends on cheap fossil-fuel materials.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The chart shows 2015 production of conventional plastics at record scale; biodegradable alternatives were a negligible share.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Producing ~380 million tonnes in one year shows a booming industry, not a declining one.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The chart is titled 'primary' (virgin) plastic production; it measures new plastic, not recycled material.

options: (A) The dependence of mass consumer culture on cheap, fossil-fuel-derived materials.
(B) The replacement of plastics by biodegradable materials by 2015, when eco-friendly substitutes had already taken over nearly the entire market.
(C) The decline of the petrochemical industry after 1980.
(D) That most plastic was produced from recycled material.
stem: The scale of production shown best illustrates which feature of the late-twentieth-century economy?
stimulus: Bar chart, 2015: global primary plastic production by polymer type, in millions of tonnes — polypropylene 68, LDPE 64, PP&A fibers 59, HDPE 52, PVC 38, PET 33, and others, totaling roughly 390 million tonnes.

explanation: The UN does not rule anyone: it is a membership organization whose agencies and forums coordinate responses to war, poverty, disease, and environmental threats — the institutional scaffolding of the globalized era.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The UN has no sovereignty over states; members join voluntarily and the General Assembly's resolutions are generally non-binding.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The headquarters houses the institution states built after 1945 to manage shared problems collectively — peacekeeping, development, health, and the environment.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Peacekeeping is only one UN function; its agencies work on refugees, health, food, children, and much more.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The UN coexists with regional bodies like the EU and African Union; it did not replace them.

options: (A) serving as a world government that directly rules member states, with the authority to overrule national governments and impose its own laws.
(B) providing a forum where states coordinate on peace, development, and shared problems like health and the environment.
(C) managing only military operations and nothing else.
(D) replacing all regional organizations such as the EU.
stem: The complex shown was built to house an institution created in 1945. Its role in the globalized era is best described as
stimulus: Photograph: the United Nations headquarters in New York City — the glass Secretariat tower and the curved General Assembly building.

explanation: With the Cold War's end, the planned economies of Eastern Europe opened to markets and foreign investment, the EU expanded eastward, and the 1990s became the high-water mark of trade liberalization — the wall's fall is the symbolic starting gun.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The 1990s saw trade barriers fall worldwide (WTO founded 1995); the wall's fall accelerated trade, it did not end it.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The EU expanded after 1989, adding Eastern European members; it did not dissolve.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The collapse of the Soviet bloc removed the Cold War's economic division, opening Eastern Europe to markets and unleashing the 1990s wave of globalization.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Korea remains divided; the wall that fell divided Germany, not Korea.

options: (A) ended all international trade, closing borders worldwide and bringing the global exchange of goods to a complete standstill.
(B) caused the European Union to dissolve.
(C) opened Eastern Europe to market economies and accelerated the integration of the world economy in the 1990s.
(D) led to the immediate reunification of Korea.
stem: The event shown is most significant for the history of globalization because the end of the Cold War
stimulus: Photograph, Berlin, November 1989: crowds stand atop the Berlin Wall at the Brandenburg Gate, waving signs reading 'OVER PEACE WEST & EAST.'

explanation: Ivy Mike — the first thermonuclear weapon, hundreds of times more powerful than the Hiroshima bomb — showed that a single weapon could now destroy a city entirely, making nuclear war a civilization-ending prospect and driving arms-control diplomacy.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Atmospheric testing continued for another decade (until the 1963 Partial Test Ban Treaty); one test did not end testing.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Hydrogen bombs have never been used in war; the Korean War ended in 1953 with conventional weapons.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The test intensified the arms race — both superpowers built thermonuclear arsenals and spent more, not less, on weapons.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The 10.4-megaton blast proved weapons of effectively unlimited power were possible, locking in a bilateral arms race and the fear of global annihilation that defined Cold War diplomacy.

options: (A) The end of all nuclear weapons testing.
(B) The use of hydrogen bombs in the Korean War.
(C) A decline in military spending by both superpowers, who decided nuclear weapons were unnecessary and dismantled their arsenals after 1952.
(D) A nuclear arms race that made the threat of annihilation global, spurring arms-control efforts and international institutions.
stem: The test shown contributed most directly to which development of the Cold War era?
stimulus: Photograph, November 1952: the mushroom cloud of the Ivy Mike test at Enewetak Atoll — the first hydrogen bomb, with a yield of 10.4 megatons.

explanation: Night lights track electrification and urban economic activity: the bright belts of North America, Europe, and Japan versus the darkness over most of Africa visualize the development gap of the 1990s more vividly than any statistic.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The brilliant North America, Europe, and Japan against a mostly dark Africa show electrified wealth concentrated in some regions while others remained dim — uneven development made visible.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Africa is the darkest continent in the image; its cities were smaller and far less electrified than those of the bright regions.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The image's whole message is inequality of light — some regions blaze while others are nearly dark.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. City lights primarily record electrification and economic activity; two equally populous cities can differ enormously in brightness depending on wealth.

options: (A) Starkly uneven development: electrification and urban wealth concentrated in North America, Europe, and Japan while much of Africa remained dim.
(B) That Africa had the world's largest and brightest cities in the 1990s, with its urban centers outshining those of North America, Europe, and Japan in the satellite image.
(C) Equal levels of electrification on every continent.
(D) That city lights measure population density rather than wealth.
stem: The image best illustrates which feature of the world economy in the 1990s?
stimulus: NASA composite of Earth's city lights, 1994–1995 (Defense Meteorological Satellite Program). North America, Europe, and Japan blaze with light; India and coastal China glow dimly; most of Africa is dark.
